description: Test your knowledge of PA GI1 | Oral Cancer and Premalignant Lesions of the Gastrointestinal Tract.

cards.text: What is the synergistic carcinogenic effect of areca nut, tobacco, and slaked lime in betel quid (paan)?
cards.answer: The combination is multiplicatively more carcinogenic than any single component. Arecoline stimulates fibroblasts, tobacco delivers carcinogens via PAHs and nitrosamines, and slaked lime enhances mucosal penetration of all carcinogens.

tip.tip: Remember: Betel quid = synergistic triad (not just additive). Areca nut alone is IARC Group 1 carcinogen.

cards.text: Compare leukoplakia and erythroplakia in terms of prevalence and malignant transformation risk.
cards.answer: Leukoplakia is more common (white patch, 5-30% transformation risk depending on dysplasia grade); erythroplakia is rare but far more dangerous (red velvety patch, ~90% of cases show severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ).

tip.tip: Red = Risky. Erythroplakia: rare but red flag. High-risk sites: floor of mouth and ventral tongue.

cards.text: Define oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF) and name its primary cause.
cards.answer: OSMF is a chronic, progressive, India-specific premalignant condition caused by areca nut alkaloids (arecoline). Pathologically, it causes subepithelial fibrosis with hyalinisation leading to ischaemia, epithelial atrophy, and dysplasia.

tip.tip: OSMF = Areca Nut Consequence. Key feature: progressive trismus (restricted mouth opening). 7-13% malignant transformation.

cards.text: What are the clinical features of oral submucous fibrosis?
cards.answer: Burning sensation in the mouth, intolerance to spices, and progressive trismus (restricted mouth opening due to submucosal fibrosis and ischaemia).

tip.tip: Trismus = Tell-tale sign of OSMF. Patient cannot open mouth properly. Examinable in MBBS.

cards.text: Describe the gross pathological features of oral squamous cell carcinoma (SCC).
cards.answer: Irregular ulcer with indurated (hardened, rolled) edges due to surrounding fibrosis; fungating/exophytic form (cauliflower-like); or infiltrative form (flat, diffuse thickening with submucosal spread). Lateral/ventral tongue and floor of mouth are most common sites.

tip.tip: Rolled edges + induration = SCC (firm on palpation). Distinguish from benign aphthous ulcer by fibrosis and firm palpation.

cards.text: What is field cancerisation and why is it clinically important in oral cancer?
cards.answer: Chronic carcinogen exposure affects the entire oral mucosa simultaneously, creating multiple independent foci of dysplasia. This explains why oral cancer patients frequently develop second primary tumours in the same field (mouth, oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus).

tip.tip: Field Cancerisation = Field of fire. One carcinogen exposure → many independent dysplastic foci → risk of recurrence/second primaries.

cards.text: How does HPV-associated oral cancer differ prognostically from tobacco/alcohol-associated SCC?
cards.answer: HPV-associated oropharyngeal SCC (especially types 16 and 18) has a better prognosis than tobacco/alcohol-driven SCC. Although E6/E7 proteins disrupt p53 and Rb, wild-type p53 is retained in some HPV-positive tumours, making them more responsive to treatment.

tip.tip: HPV = Hope. Better prognosis for young, non-smokers with oropharyngeal cancer. Tonsil and base of tongue typical sites.

cards.text: Which premalignant oral lesion is India-specific and carries a 7-13% malignant transformation rate?
cards.answer: Oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF), caused by areca nut alkaloids. It is highly prevalent in India due to betel quid (paan) chewing and is a recognized pathological entity (PA23.1) with significant malignant transformation risk.

tip.tip: OSMF = India-Specific Scourge. Areca nut + trismus + 7-13% transform rate = exam favourite.
